title: Simple Addition Worksheets for Class 2: What to Practise & In What Order + Free Quiz
meta_title: Simple Addition Worksheets for Class 2 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: What Class 2 addition worksheets should cover and in what order: 2-digit sums, regrouping, adding 3 numbers, word problems, plus a free quiz and PDF.
excerpt: A worksheet is only useful if it comes at the right time. Here is the order I put Class 2 addition practice in — from tidy 2-digit sums to word problems — with a free quiz to see where your child stands.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 2 child a page of 32 + 49 sums before they are steady on 32 + 40, and you will get a row of neat, confident, wrong answers. I see it constantly. The worksheet was fine — the timing was not. Simple addition worksheets for Class 2 only work when they arrive in the right order, one small jump at a time, so that each page practises exactly one new thing the child is ready for.

This is a map of that order. It covers everything a Class 2 child meets in written addition — two-digit sums with and without regrouping, adding three numbers, mental shortcuts and word problems — and where each piece belongs. Print the worksheet that matches where your child actually is, not where the textbook says they should be by June.

What Class 2 addition actually covers

By the NCERT Class 2 stage, a child moves well beyond the single-digit sums of Class 1. The written work for the year breaks into a handful of clear skills:

  • Adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number (24 + 5)
  • Adding two two-digit numbers with no carrying (31 + 26)
  • Adding two two-digit numbers with regrouping, or carrying (47 + 38)
  • Adding three numbers in a column
  • Mental strategies — adding tens, near-doubles, making the next ten
  • One-step and simple two-step word problems in rupees, lengths and counts

Those six lines are the whole map. A good stack of worksheets walks a child down it in order, and a bad stack jumbles them together on page one.

A worksheet progression that works

Order matters more than volume here. Ten minutes on the right page beats forty on the wrong one. This is the sequence I have watched succeed with Tier-2 city parents who practise at the kitchen table:

StageWorksheet focusExample
12-digit + 1-digit, no carry53 + 4
22-digit + 2-digit, no carry42 + 35
32-digit + 1-digit, with carry28 + 6
42-digit + 2-digit, with regrouping47 + 38
5Adding three numbers12 + 25 + 30
6Word problems (mixed)rupees, lengths, counts

Do not rush a child from stage 2 to stage 4. Stage 3 — carrying with just a single-digit second number — is the gentle bridge that teaches regrouping before both columns are in play. Skipping it is the single most common reason a child stalls on 47 + 38.

Two-digit addition, without and with regrouping

The heart of Class 2 written addition is the column method: line up ones under ones, tens under tens, add the ones column first. As long as the ones do not cross ten, the sum is tidy — 42 + 35 gives 7 ones and 7 tens, so 77, no drama.

When the ones cross ten

Regrouping is where worksheets earn their keep. In 47 + 38 the ones make 15 — that is 1 ten and 5 ones. The 5 stays in the ones place; the 1 ten is carried to the top of the tens column. Then 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens, giving 85. Children need many repetitions of exactly this move, which is why a dedicated regrouping worksheet, with the little carried 1 already faint at the top for the first few rows, is worth its weight.

Adding three numbers

Once two-digit regrouping is steady, three numbers in a column is a natural next page — and it quietly teaches a real strategy. Adding 12 + 25 + 30 is easier if a child looks for a friendly pair first: 25 and 30 are not, but rearranging to spot tens or make-ten pairs saves counting. A worksheet here should mix numbers that carry with ones that do not, so the child has to stay awake rather than switch to autopilot.

Mental strategies before the pencil

Written worksheets and mental maths are not rivals. The strongest Class 2 children reach for a mental shortcut, then use the column method to check. Three shortcuts pay off again and again:

  • Add the tens, then the ones: 46 + 30 is just 4 tens + 3 tens and 6, so 76.
  • Near-doubles: 25 + 26 is double 25 (50) and one more, 51.
  • Make the next ten: 38 + 7 — give 2 to the 38 to reach 40, then add the leftover 5, so 45.

A child who can estimate 47 + 38 as ‘about 80’ before writing anything will catch their own slips. That habit is worth more than raw speed.

Word problems: the real point of it all

Number sums are practice; word problems are the reason. Class 2 problems are short and concrete — Riya has ₹35 and her aunt gives her ₹28, how much now? The skill is not the addition, it is spotting that ‘how much now’ and ‘altogether’ and ‘in all’ are all signals to add. Give your child a few word problems on every worksheet, not a separate scary page at the end, so reading-the-maths becomes ordinary.

Common mistakes worksheets should catch

Marking the answer key is where you learn what to fix next. The recurring Class 2 slips are predictable:

  • Forgetting to carry the ten, so 47 + 38 comes out as 75 instead of 85.
  • Carrying but then forgetting to add it into the tens column.
  • Writing the whole two-digit ones total in the ones place (putting 15, not 5-carry-1).
  • Loose column alignment, so tens and ones drift and get added wrongly.

If the same error shows up three times, stop and reteach that one move with counters or a place-value chart. Do not just hand over another page of the same sums — that drills the mistake in.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight-question quiz below covers the whole progression — no-carry sums, regrouping, adding three numbers and a word problem — so you can see in two minutes which stage your child is really at. When you know that, the printable Class 2 addition worksheet at the end gives graded practice for exactly that stage, with a full answer key, so you can print the right page as often as you like.

quiz.title: Class 2 Addition Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions across the whole Class 2 addition progression — no-carry sums, regrouping, three numbers and a word problem. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: No carrying here: 2 + 5 = 7 ones and 4 + 3 = 7 tens, so 77.
The ones make 8 + 6 = 14: write 4, carry 1 ten. 2 tens + 1 = 3 tens, so 34.
Ones: 7 + 8 = 15, write 5 and carry 1. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, so 85.

questions.q: In 47 + 38, what do you carry to the tens column?
questions.explanation: The ones total 15, which is 1 ten and 5 ones. The 1 ten is carried; the 5 stays in the ones place.

questions.q: Using a mental shortcut, 46 + 30 equals what?
questions.explanation: Add the tens: 4 tens + 3 tens = 7 tens, and the 6 ones stay, so 76.

questions.q: Riya has ₹35 and her aunt gives her ₹28. How much does she have now?
questions.explanation: ‘How much now’ means add: 35 + 28. Ones 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 carry 1; tens 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, so ₹63.
In 27 + 15 the ones make 7 + 5 = 12, which crosses ten, so you carry. The others keep their ones under 10.

faq.q: What addition should a Class 2 child be able to do?
faq.a: By the end of Class 2 a child should add two-digit numbers with and without regrouping, add three numbers in a column, use simple mental shortcuts, and solve one-step word problems in rupees and everyday counts — all within 100.

faq.q: In what order should addition worksheets be given?
faq.a: Two-digit plus one-digit with no carry, then two-digit plus two-digit with no carry, then carrying with a one-digit number, then full two-digit regrouping, then adding three numbers, and finally mixed word problems. Do not skip the single-digit carrying stage.

faq.q: How do I teach carrying (regrouping) simply?
faq.a: When the ones column crosses ten, split the total into tens and ones — in 47 + 38 the ones make 15, so write the 5 and carry the 1 ten to the top of the tens column. Model it with a place-value chart or counters before moving to worksheets.

faq.q: How much addition practice a day is right for Class 2?
faq.a: About ten to fifteen focused minutes daily beats a long weekend session. Keep each worksheet to a single skill, mark it together, and reteach any mistake that appears three times rather than handing over more of the same page.
